forces.title: CCTS framework shifts focus to explicit carbon emission reduction targets
forces.description: The introduction of India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) marks a fundamental shift from the previous Perform, Achieve, Trade (PAT) scheme. While PAT focused on reducing specific energy consumption, CCTS explicitly targets greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reduction and improvement in emission intensity. This structural change reorients corporate strategies towards direct carbon performance, incentivizing widespread adoption of renewable energy and productivity improvements to meet verifiable emission reduction goals, thereby enhancing the relevance and impact of carbon markets.
forces.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

forces.title: India's net-zero 2070 and 500 GW renewable targets boost carbon solutions
forces.description: India's ambitious climate commitments, including achieving net-zero emissions by 2070 and 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030, act as a significant tailwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. These national targets necessitate widespread decarbonization efforts across all sectors, increasing the demand for carbon credits and making CCUS solutions more critical for hard-to-abate industries. The policy drive creates a robust regulatory and investment environment, encouraging companies to actively participate in carbon markets and invest in emission reduction technologies to meet their obligations and contribute to national goals.

forces.title: Regulatory framework for CCTS strengthens, accelerating India's carbon market
forces.description: The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has progressed significantly from concept to implementation, with regulatory notifications and procedures for measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) established by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). This structured framework, administered by a government-based organization, ensures transparency and enables tradable carbon certificates for verified GHG emission reductions. This robust regulatory support provides a strong tailwind for the carbon markets, creating a credible compliance mechanism and fostering confidence among participants, driving engagement and investment in carbon management solutions.
forces.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

forces.title: Declining decarbonization technology costs and rising carbon prices boost investment
forces.description: The rapidly decreasing costs of decarbonization technologies, including solar, wind, battery storage, carbon capture, hydrogen, and electrification, coupled with an expected increase in carbon prices, presents a significant tailwind. This economic dynamic makes investing in emission reduction solutions more financially viable and attractive, as abatement costs fall below the price of carbon credits. Such a trend creates strong incentives for companies to undertake proactive decarbonization measures, driving demand for innovative technologies and increasing participation and liquidity within the carbon markets.
forces.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

forces.title: Increased fossil fuel generation drives demand for carbon credits and CCUS
forces.description: A rising share of fossil fuel-based electricity generation in India directly increases overall carbon emissions. This necessitates greater efforts to meet emission reduction targets, thereby boosting demand for carbon credits and Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) solutions. As India continues to rely on thermal power to meet its growing energy needs, the imperative for carbon management technologies and market-based mechanisms intensifies, providing a sustained tailwind for the IN010309 sub-industry by creating a larger pool of obligated emitters seeking compliance solutions.

forces.title: Rising HRC steel prices increase CCUS infrastructure capital costs
forces.description: Higher HRC steel prices negatively impact the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry by directly increasing the capital costs associated with constructing CCUS infrastructure. Steel is a key material for pipelines, storage facilities, and other components of carbon capture projects. This rise in input costs makes new CCUS projects more expensive, potentially hindering their financial viability and deployment. Consequently, higher steel prices act as a headwind by slowing the expansion of critical infrastructure needed for large-scale carbon removal and utilization efforts.

forces.title: Rising natural gas prices increase CCUS operational costs and reduce demand
forces.description: Increasing natural gas prices act as a headwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry by raising the energy costs for CCUS operations. Carbon capture facilities are energy-intensive, and higher fuel prices directly impact their operational expenses. Moreover, rising natural gas prices can accelerate the transition away from gas-fired power, potentially reducing the long-term pool of emissions associated with natural gas that CCUS solutions are designed to address. This dual impact of increased costs and reduced future demand negatively affects the sub-industry's growth prospects.

forces.title: Higher electricity prices increase operational costs for CCUS facilities
forces.description: Rising electricity prices pose a significant headwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. Carbon capture, utilization, and storage facilities are highly energy-intensive, requiring substantial electricity for their operations. Therefore, an increase in electricity costs directly translates to higher operational expenses for CCUS projects. This escalation in operating costs can erode profit margins, reduce the financial attractiveness of new projects, and ultimately hinder the broader deployment of CCUS technologies, impacting the economic viability of carbon management solutions.

forces.title: INR depreciation raises costs for imported CCUS equipment and international credits
forces.description: An increase in the USD/INR exchange rate, signifying INR depreciation, acts as a headwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. It directly increases the cost of importing specialized CCUS equipment and advanced technologies, making project implementation more expensive. Additionally, for companies needing to purchase international carbon credits or trade in USD-denominated markets, INR depreciation raises the cost of these transactions. This currency effect results in a cost squeeze for decarbonization projects and can hinder the adoption of advanced carbon management solutions.
forces.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

forces.title: Ambiguity in carbon market liquidity and price discovery creates uncertainty
forces.description: A key risk for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry is the current ambiguity surrounding market liquidity and the process of price discovery for carbon credits. Without established institutions like exchanges, aggregators, verifiers, and market makers, confidence in pricing and trade volumes remains low. This uncertainty hinders investment decisions, impedes the effective functioning of the market, and can delay the widespread adoption of carbon management strategies. Addressing these market readiness challenges is crucial for fostering a stable and predictable environment for carbon trading and CCUS deployment.
forces.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

forces.title: Fiscal deficit threatens government support for CCUS and carbon market development
forces.description: A rising fiscal deficit poses a key risk to the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. It signals government financial strain, which can lead to reduced public investment, subsidies, or policy support for green initiatives and CCUS projects. Fiscal tightening can delay funding for carbon market infrastructure and demonstration projects, increase borrowing costs for private ventures, and create overall macroeconomic uncertainty. This directly impacts the financial viability and deployment pace of carbon management solutions, highlighting the sensitivity of the sector to government fiscal health and budgetary allocations.

forces.title: Declining GDP growth dampens demand for carbon management solutions
forces.description: A falling trend in India's GDP Annual Growth Rate acts as a headwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. Decelerated economic activity typically leads to decreased industrial production and overall energy consumption. This reduction in activity directly correlates with lower carbon emissions, consequently diminishing the need and demand for carbon management solutions like credits and CCUS. Slower economic expansion can delay industrial decarbonization projects and reduce the overall volume of carbon credits traded, impacting the sub-industry's growth and profitability.

forces.title: Rising renewable capacity reduces long-term demand for carbon credits and CCUS
forces.description: An increasing share of renewable installed capacity in the energy mix, while positive for overall decarbonization, creates an inverse impact on the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. A cleaner energy mix reduces the overall carbon footprint of the power sector, directly lessening the long-term demand for carbon credits and the need for CCUS solutions to abate emissions from power generation. As renewables scale up and displace fossil fuels, the necessity for market-based carbon instruments and capture technologies tied to conventional power production diminishes.

forces.title: Manufacturing IIP growth drives industrial emissions and demand for carbon solutions
forces.description: A rising Manufacturing IIP (Index of Industrial Production) signifies increased industrial activity and production across India. This economic expansion invariably leads to higher energy consumption and associated carbon emissions from the manufacturing sector. Consequently, this boosts the demand for carbon credits and Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) solutions, as industries seek to comply with emission reduction targets under frameworks like CCTS or mitigate their environmental impact. This sustained industrial growth provides a strong tailwind for the IN010309 sub-industry by expanding its potential customer base.

forces.title: Increased government capital expenditure stimulates demand for CCUS and carbon markets
forces.description: Rising government capital expenditure, particularly when directed towards green infrastructure or industrial decarbonization, acts as a significant tailwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. This increased public spending can directly stimulate demand for CCUS projects and provide crucial funding for their development and deployment. It also supports the broader development of carbon market infrastructure. Government investment signals strong policy commitment, reduces investment risk for private players, and accelerates the adoption of carbon management solutions across various sectors to meet national climate goals.

forces.title: Improved regulatory efficiency enhances operational ease for carbon markets and CCUS
forces.description: A rising regulatory efficiency sub-index, indicating an improved ease of doing business, serves as a tailwind for the Carbon Markets & CCUS sub-industry. Enhanced regulatory clarity and streamlined processes reduce operational friction and compliance costs for companies engaged in carbon markets and CCUS projects. This supportive environment encourages greater investment and activity within the sector by lowering barriers to entry and operation, fostering innovation, and accelerating the deployment of carbon management solutions. It strengthens market confidence and predictability for all stakeholders.

viewpoints.title: India's CCTS transforms carbon performance into economic value for companies
viewpoints.description: Kapil Bansal of EY-Parthenon views India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) as a transformative mechanism that converts carbon performance into economic value. Companies outperforming emission reduction targets can monetize carbon credits, improving their financial bottom line, while underperformers must procure them, making it a cost item. This scheme is distinct from previous energy-saving focused mechanisms like PAT, explicitly targeting greenhouse gas emission reductions and intensity improvements through productivity and renewable energy adoption, accelerating India's decarbonization efforts and enhancing ESG credibility.
viewpoints.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

viewpoints.title: Companies integrating net-zero strategies into operations gain financial and strategic benefits
viewpoints.description: According to Kapil Bansal of EY-Parthenon, companies that embed net-zero strategies and actively participate in carbon credit trading will realize significant financial and strategic advantages. Monetizing surplus carbon credits improves profitability and allows reinvestment in decarbonization technologies. Strategically, it ensures compliance, enhances ESG credibility with investors and stakeholders, and strengthens brand positioning. This proactive approach helps firms prepare for evolving regulatory landscapes and capitalize on the economic value generated from verifiable emission reductions, fostering continuous improvement in environmental performance and market valuation.
viewpoints.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

viewpoints.title: India's carbon market implementation shows strong intent but faces market and readiness hurdles
viewpoints.description: Kapil Bansal of EY-Parthenon notes a significant shift from 'intent to implementation' in India's carbon market and CCTS framework, with considerable regulatory work completed. However, market readiness faces challenges including ambiguity in liquidity and price discovery, and the need for robust implementing institutions like exchanges, aggregators, and verifiers. Company readiness also lags in technology adoption for accurate reporting and capital availability for decarbonization measures, indicating a dual challenge of developing both the market infrastructure and corporate capacity for effective carbon trading.
viewpoints.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

viewpoints.title: Innovation, technology, and capital markets crucial for accelerated decarbonization and market maturity
viewpoints.description: Kapil Bansal of EY-Parthenon asserts that innovation, technology, and robust capital markets are pivotal for accelerating India's decarbonization efforts. The declining costs of clean technologies (solar, wind, battery storage, CCUS, hydrogen) coupled with an expected rise in carbon prices, will incentivize early investment in decarbonization. Companies must digitalize operational data, develop carbon strategies, and track greening initiatives to gain competitive valuations. Future market maturity depends on easier capital access, indigenous R&D, localization of technology, and building infrastructure like hydrogen/CCUS pipelines through public-private partnerships, supported by stringent governance.
viewpoints.source_title: How India Inc. can accelerate decarbonization with CCTS

viewpoints.title: Indian companies excel in emissions reduction, leveraging decarbonization for financial gains
viewpoints.description: IBEF highlights that Indian companies are demonstrating strong performance in emissions reporting and reduction, outperforming global averages. This proactive approach to decarbonization is translating into significant financial gains for these companies, showcasing a substantial, yet untapped, potential within sustainability and AI-driven innovations. The trend underscores a growing recognition of the economic benefits associated with environmental stewardship and the adoption of clean technologies, positioning India Inc. favorably in the global transition towards a low-carbon economy and boosting confidence in carbon markets and CCUS solutions.

viewpoints.title: Cement industry abatement costs to fall below carbon prices by 2036, incentivizing early investment
viewpoints.description: EY analysis suggests that the Indian cement industry will find it financially advantageous to invest in decarbonization technologies sooner rather than later. Projections indicate that the cost of abating CO2 emissions will drop below US$19/tCO2 by 2036, while Indian carbon prices are expected to surpass this level. This divergence creates a strong economic incentive for early adopters, allowing them to realize significant cost savings by avoiding the higher costs associated with purchasing carbon credit certificates, reinforcing the viability and profitability of decarbonization initiatives within the sector.
viewpoints.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

viewpoints.title: Chlor-Alkali sector poised for decarbonization investment as abatement costs drop below carbon prices
viewpoints.description: EY's analysis indicates that the Indian Chlor-Alkali industry should begin investing in decarbonization technologies now. By 2031, the cost of CO2 abatement is projected to fall below US$15/tCO2, while Indian carbon prices are expected to rise above this level. This offers significant cost savings by reducing reliance on carbon credit purchases, thereby accelerating incentives for the sector. As abatement technologies scale and mature, further cost reductions are anticipated, enhancing the financial attractiveness of decarbonization and boosting the economic viability of the carbon market for this industry.
viewpoints.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the cement sector must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
Despite emission reduction targets, projected production growth in the cement sector will lead to increased absolute emissions, necessitating carbon solutions.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: Decarbonizing below the carbon price yields cost savings. The cost of decarbonization is projected to drop below US$19/tCO2 by 2036, while carbon prices are expected to rise above, making abatement profitable.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the cement sector is an average 2-6% reduction in emission intensity over baseline during the compliance period. This reduction translates to 8.67 MMT CO2e reduction by FY27, assuming constant installed capacity as per FY2023-2024. The total potential net increase in CO2e for cement sector for FY27 is 31.54 MMT, based on production forecast, indicating a significant demand for carbon solutions.
market_sizing.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the aluminum sector must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
The expected effects of carbon pricing under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) have already influenced export shares to the EU, increasing the incentive for domestic decarbonization.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: The cost of decarbonization is projected to drop below US$34/tCO2 by 2037 in a pessimistic scenario, while carbon prices are expected to rise above, making abatement profitable and incentivizing early investment.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the aluminum sector is an average 4-7% reduction in emission intensity over baseline during the compliance period. This reduction translates to approximately 4.3 MMT CO2e reduction by FY27, assuming constant installed capacity as per FY2023-2024. The sector faces a potential net decrease of ~1.74 MMT of CO2 emissions during the compliance period based on production forecast, indicating an opportunity for generating carbon credits.
market_sizing.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the caustic soda sector must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
The caustic soda sector is growing at a CAGR of 6.2%, implying increasing absolute emissions that require abatement to meet intensity targets.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: The cost of decarbonization is projected to drop below US$15/tCO2 by 2031 (normative scenario), while Indian carbon prices are expected to rise above this level, creating strong financial incentives for abatement.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the caustic soda (chlor-alkali) sector is an average 6-9% reduction in emission intensity over baseline during the compliance period. This reduction translates to approximately 0.66 MMT CO2e reduction by FY27. This represents the compliance obligation amount. The sector operates at ~80% capacity utilization, with production growing at a CAGR of 6.2%.
market_sizing.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the paper industry must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
Despite emission reduction targets, projected production growth in the paper industry will lead to increased absolute emissions, necessitating carbon solutions.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: The cost of decarbonization is projected to drop below US$15/tCO2 by 2029 (normative scenario), while Indian carbon prices are expected to rise above this level, creating strong financial incentives for abatement.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the paper industry is an average 4-9% reduction in emission intensity over baseline during the compliance period. This reduction translates to approximately 750 KT CO2e reduction by FY27, assuming constant installed capacity as per FY2023-2024. The sector projects a potential net increase of ~240 KT of CO2e emissions during the compliance period, based on production forecast, indicating a need for carbon solutions.

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the refinery sector must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
India's refining capacity is set for significant expansion, leading to increased absolute emissions that will require carbon management solutions despite intensity reductions.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: The cost of decarbonization is projected to drop below US$17/tCO2 by 2033 (normative scenario), while Indian carbon prices are expected to rise above this level, creating financial incentives for abatement.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the refinery sector is an emission intensity reduction of 2-6% over baseline during the compliance period. This translates to approximately 3.3 MMT CO2e reduction by FY27, assuming constant installed capacity as per FY2023-2024. India's refining capacity is projected to grow from 257 MMTPA to 310 MMTPA by 2028, and oil demand is expected to reach one million barrels by 2045, indicating significant future emissions requiring management.
market_sizing.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: Obligated entities in the textile sector must achieve targeted emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct decarbonization investments.
The robust growth of the textile and apparel industry will result in higher overall emissions, necessitating continuous decarbonization efforts to meet intensity targets.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: The current cost of abatement for the textile industry is ~2.6 US$/tCO2e, indicating that emission reductions are already cost-saving initiatives. Avoiding decarbonization would incur a financial impact of INR53-59 crore from 2026-2030.

market_sizing.methodology: CCTS target for the textile sector is an emission intensity reduction of 4-12% over baseline during the compliance period. This translates to approximately 1.6 MMT CO2e reduction by FY27, assuming constant installed capacity as per FY2023-2024. The sector is projected to grow at a 10% CAGR, reaching US$350 billion by 2030, which implies continued demand for energy and thus emissions that require management.
market_sizing.source_title: How CCTS is accelerating India Inc.’s race to decarbonize

demand_drivers.description: The CCTS framework will mandate emission intensity reductions, driving demand for carbon credits or direct abatement solutions in the iron and steel sector.

pnl_drivers.driver: Cost of decarbonization vs. carbon price
pnl_drivers.description: Investing in decarbonization technologies now will lead to significant cost savings in the future as abatement costs are expected to fall below rising carbon prices, enhancing profitability.

market_sizing.methodology: EY analysis indicates that for the iron and steel industry, the cost of abating CO2 emissions is projected to fall below Indian carbon prices by 2035 in a pessimistic scenario, with the cost dropping below US$30/tCO2. This forecast suggests that early investment in decarbonization technologies will yield significant cost savings by overcoming future carbon credit purchasing costs.
